September 28, 2026

Chair Laura V. Swett
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street, N.E.
Washington, D.C, 20426

Dear Chair Swett:

We write regarding BlackRock’s subsidiary Global Infrastructure Partners’ (GIP) application
before the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to acquire AES Corporation (AES),
a publicly traded energy company that owns two regulated utility companies in Ohio and Indiana
(AES Ohio and AES Indiana).1 This application, submitted by GIP alongside a consortium of co-
investors,2 comes as private funds and private equity firms increasingly buy up public utility
companies. The private equity industry’s involvement in the public utility market has significant
implications for consumers’ energy costs at a time when Americans are facing record high utility
bills.3

Federal law generally authorizes FERC to approve mergers, acquisitions, and sales of public
utilities only if FERC finds that the proposed transaction is “consistent with the public interest”
and will not result in the “cross-subsidization” of an associated non-utility company.4 GIP’s
application fails to establish how this merger is consistent with the public interest and leaves
open the possibility that the merger could be used to cross-subsidize other non-utility lines of
BlackRock’s businesses, all while unfairly passing on transaction costs to their consumers. Based
on our review of the application filed by BlackRock’s GIP and its co-applicants, we urge FERC
to deny the merger.

  I.    A FERC-approved transaction must be “consistent with the public interest.”

Under the Federal Power Act, FERC is responsible for approving sales, leases, dispositions,
mergers, consolidations, purchases, and acquisitions of public utilities. The statute makes clear
that FERC, after receiving an application for a proposed transaction, “shall approve [a] proposed
disposition, consolidation, acquisition or change in control” of a public utility “if it finds that the
proposed transaction will be consistent with the public interest.”5 To assess if a merger is
consistent with the public interest, the Commission requires applicants to “...include a general

    a. GIP’s acquisition of AES may increase rates for consumers, contrary to the public
       interest.

We are concerned that GIP’s acquisition of AES will increase rates for consumers. GIP is a
private equity firm owned by BlackRock, a global asset manager. Private equity’s business
model is well-documented: firms purchase a company or companies, often through leveraged
buy outs, and take steps to cut costs while boosting value to shareholders – the consequences of
which consistently fall on consumers.7 GIP’s application to purchase AES claims this merger
“will have no adverse effect on rates” and “the transaction will substitute a group of shareholders
with alternative investors but will have no effect on the utility operations of the AES Utilities.”8
This declaration fails to consider how the new ownership structure would likely affect AES’s
incentives. In reality, however, GIP could increase rates to meet its standard rate of return for
shareholders.

GIP’s private equity funds typically target an internal rate of return (IRR) of 15-20 percent
across a five year period, and at times have achieved an IRR upwards of 20 percent.9 However, a
study of U.S. publicly traded utilities showed that over the last century, utility companies have
delivered an average and median return of 10.4 percent.10 In other words, the evidence already
suggests a potential mismatch between the rate of return traditionally expected by GIP and the
returns generated by AES Corp – raising concerns over whether GIP will resort to private
equity’s tried and true tactics, such as rate hikes, in order to bridge the shortfall.

A potential spike in rate hikes is particularly concerning in this case because AES Ohio and AES
Indiana have repeatedly asked for rate hikes in recent years. In June, the Indiana Utility
Regulatory Commission (IURC) “approved a $71 million electricity rate increase for AES
Indiana customers.”11 This came after an approved rate hike in 2024.12 Notably, as of September
2026, the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission voted to reconsider the rate increase previously

residential customers have seen approximately a 47 percent increase in their utility bills. 14 AES
Ohio similarly was approved to increase rates in 2020 and 2024, and is now pursuing a multi-
year rate plan that, if approved, would increase utility bills for customers by over $6 a month in
2027.15 Ohioans are already paying 50 percent more for electricity than they were five years
ago.16 This trend seems likely to be exacerbated if these firms were under the control of private
equity firms designed to maximize profits.

This concern is particularly significant in Indiana, where unprecedented proposed data-center
loads are already requiring substantial new generation and transition infrastructure.17 The
Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) itself has described the surge in large-load
requests, driven in significant part by data centers, as “unprecedented.”18 FERC should
specifically determine whether any AES Indiana infrastructure investments associated with
affiliated or commonly owned data-center interest could shift costs or risks to existing Indiana
ratepayers.

Furthermore, government officials have raised concerns in the past about BlackRock’s and its
affiliates’ business model, and its impact on utility customers’ rates. In 2025, for example, an
administrative judge in Minnesota issued findings relating to Blackrock’s application to acquire
energy and utility company ALLETE that underscored the dangers within private equity’s
business model. The judge warned that GIP’s purported “disavowal of ‘stereotypical’ private
equity tactics such as ‘debt leveraging, cost-cutting operational changes, and asset sales’ to
achieve their desired returns lacks credibility,” given that it was highly unlikely GIP could
achieve their target rate of return without rate hikes.19

     b. GIP’s proposed acquisition of AES comes as BlackRock expands its ownership of energy
       and utility companies and could reduce competition.

When evaluating this merger’s effect on competition, FERC must examine the transaction within
the broader context of BlackRock’s expanding ownership of the country’s energy and utility
infrastructure. In 2025, FERC voted to renew BlackRock’s Blanket Authorization for an
additional three years, which allows the company to own up to 20 percent of voting securities in
public utilities.20 The Commission did so even as former Republican chairman of FERC, Mark
Christie, noted that “one threat is that asset managers, like BlackRock, will use their ownership
of competing assets to exert market power in wholesale energy, capacity, and ancillary services
markets.”21

BlackRock’s renewed Blanket Authorization may change the competitive landscape of the utility
company marketplace in a way that the traditional market power analysis does not fully capture.
The Commission itself noted when approving BlackRock’s Blanket Authorization: “...we have
some concern that the breadth of Applicants’ holdings under their Blanket Authorizations, along
with their growing controlling holdings in GIM {Global Infrastructure Management LLC, owner
of GIP}, ALLETE and other public utility assets, may allow for a novel degree of influence over
both their non-controlling and controlling holdings.”22 As consumer advocates noted in their
letter scrutinizing this merger, “with BlackRock’s effort to control yet another utility holding
company with over a million franchised utility customers, the Commission can no longer explain
away its ‘concern’ about BlackRock’s holdings under Blanket Authorizations conflicting with its
‘growing controlling holdings’ in public utilities.”23

GIP and its co-applicants are completely silent on the issue when discussing the merger’s effect
on competition, despite BlackRock’s Blanket Authorization and mounting acquisitions of utility
companies, such as the purchase of utility companies in Wisconsin and Indiana and GIP in
2024.24 FERC must examine GIP’s application and effects on competition within this broader
context.

 II. A FERC-approved transaction cannot result in “cross-subsidization” that is inconsistent
with the public interest.

The Federal Power Act also makes clear that FERC must only approve transactions that “will
not result in cross-subsidization of a non-utility associate company or the pledge or encumbrance
of utility assets for the benefit of an associate company, unless the Commission determines that
the cross-subsidization, pledge, or encumbrance will be consistent with the public interest.”25
According to the Commission’s requirements, a merger application must provide “an
explanation, with appropriate evidentiary support for such explanation…: (1) Of how applicants
are providing assurance, based on facts and circumstances known to them or that are reasonably
foreseeable, that the proposed transaction will not result in, at the time of the transaction or in the
future, cross-subsidization of a non-utility associate company or pledge or encumbrance of utility
assets for the benefit of an associate company, including: (i) Disclosure of existing pledges
and/or encumbrances of utility assets…”26

However, GIP’s application mostly restates FERC’s requirements and provides no evidentiary
explanation on how they arrive at the conclusion that the merger would not result in cross-
subsidization. The application fails to discuss facts that are “reasonably foreseeable” for private
equity ownership, such as refinancing, recapitalizations, changes in dividend policy, changes in
servicing arrangements between utility and non-utility affiliates.27 The application fails to even
explicitly affirm there are no existing pledges of utility assets already within the BlackRock
enterprise.28

In reality, there are many ways in which the merger could result in cross-subsidization. One
glaring example is BlackRock’s extensive ownership of data centers across the U.S.29 GIP owned
40 data centers when they filed the AES merger application in May 2026.30 Then, in late July,
GIP, the Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure Partnership (another BlackRock affiliate), and
investment firm MGX collectively acquired 100 percent of Aligned Data Centers, which owns at
least 20 data centers across the United States, including two in Ohio.31

 Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity and can require utility companies to spend
hundreds of millions of dollars on upgrades to the grid’s infrastructure to adequately serve them.
If this merger is approved, BlackRock and GIP would have financial interests on both sides of
the equation: GIP would control AES Ohio and AES Indiana, while also having significant
control over data centers in the area. This creates the incentive for AES Ohio or AES Indiana to
construct or accelerate infrastructure investments that mainly benefit an affiliated data center,
while potentially placing the costs of the upgrades on their customers. Even worse, if a data
center fails, customers may continue paying for the unnecessary upgrades via increased utility
bills. In effect, this ownership structure risks privatizing the financial benefit of upgrading AES’s
utility infrastructure among BlackRock and its affiliates, while potentially socializing the costs to
AES’s utility customers.

In addition to providing no meaningful evidence, the applicants even requested a partial waiver
from the requirement to submit “organizational charts depicting the applicant’s current and
proposed post-transaction corporate structures.”32 The applicants stated that they only provided
the organizational charts “to the extent necessary…to include only those parent companies,
energy subsidiaries, and energy affiliates that are relevant to the Transaction.”33 The
organizational charts provided only offer a visual representation of AES Corp owning AES Ohio
and AES Indiana with and without the new consortium of investors led by BlackRock’s GIP.34
They fail to list any other affiliate within the corporate structure of BlackRock or its co-
applicants that may stand to benefit from this merger, including the data centers discussed above.

The failure to adequately demonstrate this merger would not result in cross-subsidization is a
fundamental flaw in the application. In Order No. 669-A, which further details an applicant’s
requirements to demonstrate there would be no cross-subsidization, the Commission noted that
“the applicant bears the burden of proof to demonstrate that customers will be protected.”35

III. Conclusion

FERC has a critical role to play as a backstop to BlackRock’s attempt to enmesh itself in the
utility industry as electricity rates are increasing for American households. Last year alone,

U.S. Energy Information Administration.36 This came as electric utilities across the nation have
requested rate increases totaling $71.2 billion through 2028.37

BlackRock/GIP has not fully disclosed its energy and data-center affiliates or provided
enforceable assurances that existing utility customers will be protected from the costs and risks
of infrastructure constructed to serve affiliated large-load customers. The absence of this
transparency and these protections leaves fundamental public-interest and cross-subsidization
concerns unresolved.

BlackRock’s GIP and its consortium of investors failed to demonstrate how the proposed merger
is consistent with the public interest or prohibits cross-subsidization. We therefore urge FERC to
reject this application.
